en: The formal motion for full ordination: "Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from taking life;

even so, I, named so-and-so, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, shall abstain from taking life. Thus, by this first factor, I train in accordance with, conform to, and emulate the training of those noble Arhats.

"Just as those noble ones, the Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, have abstained from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants;

even so, I, [name], for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, shall abstain from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants. By this fifth limb, I train after the training of those noble Arhats, I conform to it, and I imitate it."
Thus a second and a third time.
Thereafter, a monk should be requested;
he who announces it in this manner [is to be appointed].
The monk who is to announce must ask.
If he announces without having asked about the rules of proper conduct (*āsamudācārika-dharma*), he incurs an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*).
Afterwards, the monk who has announced must report it.
Furthermore, it should be announced in this way:

when the entire Saṅgha has assembled and is seated together, one should perform the proper salutation at the feet of those who sit at the edge of the assembly, stand in a crouching position at the end of the row of elders, join the palms in añjali, and say these words: "Venerable sirs, please attend to me."

This person, named so-and-so, desiring the going forth under the preceptor named so-and-so— a householder clad in white garments with hair and beard unshorn— seeks to go forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya. This person, named so-and-so, having had his hair and beard shorn and having donned saffron robes under the preceptor named so-and-so, will go forth from the home to the homeless state out of perfect faith in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Everything should be stated:
"If he is pure," and "If they say so, it is well."
If they do not say so, they become guilty of an offense (*sātisāra*).
Thereafter, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should be requested;
and he should be requested in this manner:
Having performed the proper salutation and standing before him in a squatting posture, this should be said: "Pay attention, Preceptor!
I, so-and-so by name, request the Preceptor as my Upādhyāya."
"May the teacher be my preceptor;
through the preceptor of the teachers, I shall go forth.
Thus a second and a third time.
But at the third recitation, one should say, "Preceptor.
Thereafter, he should be ordained;
and furthermore, he should be ordained in this manner.
Pay heed, Preceptor!
I, who am named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion.

I go for refuge to the Saṃgha, the foremost of assemblies. I follow into the homeless life after that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Sovereign of the Śākyas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. I cast off the marks of a householder.
"I take up the mark of renunciation.
Thus a second and a third time.
Thereafter, the hair should be shaved off.
He also has his hair shaved off.
The Blessed One said:
"A topknot should be left."
Thereafter, he should be questioned. And his topknot (śikhā) should be untied. If he says "no," he should be told: "In that case, go."
He speaks thus:
she must first be made to descend,
and only after that should he bathe her.
If it is the cold season, he should bathe with warm water;
if it is the hot season, with cool water.
Thereafter, having abandoned the marks of a householder, I desire the marks of one who has gone forth.
The preceptor must give the saffron robes;
he, in turn, must receive them by prostrating at the preceptor’s feet. Thereafter, the preceptor must help him put them on.
And he should examine whether he is not lacking in sexual characteristics,
or whether he possesses both sets of sexual characteristics.
The Blessed One said, "It should be examined.
They, having stripped them naked, examined them.
The Blessed One said, "It should not be examined by stripping them naked."
Moreover, while putting it on, he should examine it without being distracted;
thereafter, a monk who bestows upon him the refuges and the precepts of training should be requested.

Having performed the proper salutation toward him, sitting before him in a squatting posture and raising his joined palms, he should speak as follows: "Pay attention, Venerable Sir! I, who am named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost among two-legged beings;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost among things free from passion."
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies.
Thus a second and a third time. At the third utterance, it should be said:
The preceptors maintain the dharmas that constitute the qualities of a novice; therefore, the training rules must be caused to be undertaken.
Furthermore, they should be caused to be undertaken in this manner:
"Pay attention, Preceptor!"

Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life; even so, I, [name], for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I train after them, follow their example, and imitate the training of those noble Arhats.
Just as those noble Arhats [abstain] for as long as life lasts from taking what is not given, unchaste conduct,
false speech,
and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants,

Having abandoned dancing, singing, instrumental music, wearing garlands, perfumes, ointments, and cosmetics, using high and luxurious beds, eating at improper times, and accepting gold and silver— they abstain from accepting gold and silver—
so too do I, [named so-and-so], for as long as life lasts, abandon taking what is not given and unchastity...
False speech,
the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants,
dancing, singing, music, the wearing of garlands, perfumes, ointments, and cosmetics, and the use of high and luxurious beds and seats.

Having abandoned eating at improper times and the acceptance of gold and silver, I abstain from the acceptance of gold and silver; by this tenth limb, I train after the training of those noble Arhats, I conform to it, and I imitate it.
Thus a second and a third time.
The formal act of full ordination (upasampadā) is to be performed.
Then, if he has reached twenty years of age, his bowl and robes must be sought out;
a monk who will act as the private instructor must be requested;
and a monk who will perform the formal ritual act must be requested.
Those who shall enter the mandala—
once the entire Saṅgha has assembled and sat down, or in a final group of ten within the mandala— should be made to perform the *sāmīcī* three times.
Having been made to perform two *sāmīcīs* either by prostrating with the five points of the body touching the ground or by falling at the feet, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should then be requested.
If he is a preceptor, he is indeed a preceptor;
if he is a teacher, he is indeed a teacher; if he is a venerable one, he is indeed a venerable one.
Furthermore, he should request it in this manner:
having performed the proper salutation toward the preceptor, sitting on his heels before him with his heels touching, and raising his joined palms, he should speak as follows:
"Pay attention, Preceptor."
I, [name], request the preceptor as my preceptor.
May the preceptor be my preceptor;
through the preceptor I shall attain completion.
In this manner, it should be repeated a second and a third time.
However, on the third occasion, if the person is an *ācārya* or a *bhadanta*, one should say "Upādhyāya.
Thereafter, the robes should also be set down.
If they are already cut, it should nevertheless be set aside thus:
"Pay attention, Preceptor!
I, named so-and-so, resolve upon this robe as a *saṃghāṭī*."
This robe has been determined as fit for use. Thus a second and a third time.
Pay attention, Preceptor!
"I, [name], resolve upon this robe, the upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*), as allowable.
This robe is determined, allowable, and fit for use.
Thus it should be said a second and a third time.
Even if they are torn, they should still be worn.
Pay attention, Preceptor:
I consecrate this robe-cloth as a *saṃghāṭī*.
I desire to prepare nine [portions],
namely two and a half maṇḍalakas;
having sat down without hindrance, I shall distribute them.
I shall cut it, I shall join it together, I shall knot it, I shall sew it.
I shall preserve it, or I shall have it sewn by an attendant;
or I shall make it into a rain-cloak as the occasion requires. This robe is for use.
In this way, it should be said a second and a third time:
"Pay attention, Preceptor;
I, named so-and-so, resolve upon this robe as an upper garment."
I desire to perform the sevenfold [rite]. Having sat down without obstruction upon the two and a half maṇḍalakas,
I shall spread it out and cut it.
I shall join it together; I shall stitch it; I shall sew it.
I shall protect it; I shall attach it to the lining.
"I shall make this robe-cloth into an article of use according to the conditions.
This should be said a second and a third time.
"Pay attention, Preceptor!"
I, [name], designate this robe as an inner garment (*antarvāsa*). I desire to make it into a five-panel robe with a half-circle border,
provided there is no obstacle to sitting down.
I shall cross over,
I shall cut through,
I shall completely extinguish.
I shall join it together; I shall sew it; I shall protect it; I shall attach it to the lining; or I shall act according to the circumstances.
"This robe is for use.
This should be said a second and a third time.
Thereafter, the bowl should be displayed before the Saṅgha.
Thinking, "This shall be his bowl, whether it be a washing bowl or an alms bowl," he should then perform the formal consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, it should be consecrated in this manner:
Having placed it in the left hand and covered it with the right hand, one should say: "Pay attention, Preceptor!
I, [name], take possession of this bowl—the vessel of the sages, the vessel for alms, for the purpose of using it for food.
This should be said a second and a third time as well.
Thereafter, having set aside the formalities of listening, he should be made to stand facing the assembly with his hands joined in *añjali* as a mark of respect during the formalities of seeing.
Then, the officiating monk (*karmakāraka*) should ask:
"Who, indeed, is your teacher?"
"Private instructor of one named so-and-so"—
he who has been requested must say, "I am indeed [named] so-and-so.
Thereafter, he should be encouraged.
"Are you able, [Name], to provide secret instruction for [Name] under the tutelage of a preceptor named [Name]?
He should reply, "I am able."
Then, the monk Karmakāka should make the formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This monk named So-and-so is capable of instructing in private the monk named So-and-so."
With the preceptor named so-and-so.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and if the Saṃgha should permit and authorize it,
let the Saṃgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the private instructor for the monk named so-and-so.
"This monk, named so-and-so, shall give the private instruction to [the candidate] named so-and-so, with [the preceptor] named so-and-so as his preceptor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

Thereafter, the monk acting as the private instructor, having caused himself to be made to assume a respectful posture and having had [the candidate] sit in the *utkuṭika* position with palms joined in reverence, should speak as follows:

Listen, venerable one; the time for truth has come, the time for reality. Whatever I ask you, you should, being skilled in the true nature of things, speak what is real as real and clarify what is unreal as unreal.
Are you a male? A male. Are you endowed with the male faculty? Endowed.
"Are you twenty years of age?
"I am twenty years of age.
"Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?"
"Are they complete? Are your mother and father alive?
If he says, "They are alive," you should say:
If he asks, "Have you been permitted by your mother and father?", one should say, "I have.
If he asks, "Are you a slave? Are you a prisoner? Are you someone who must not speak?", [one should answer accordingly].
Is he not one who has been brought away by force?
Is he not one who has been sold? Is he not a royal soldier?
Are you not a criminal against the king?
Are you not one who has committed an offense against the king? Have you not yourself performed, or caused to be performed, any act that is an offense against the king?
Are you a thief with a banner raised?
Are you not a eunuch, a paṇḍaka, or one lacking sexual organs?
Are you not a hermaphrodite? Are you not a defiler of nuns?
Are you not a matricide?
Are you not a parricide? Are you not a slayer of an Arhat? Are you not a schismatic of the Sangha?
Are you not one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind?
Are you not a non-Buddhist?
Are you not one who has entered the fold of non-Buddhists?
Are you not one who lives in communion through theft? Are you not one who lives in a separate communion? Are you not one who does not live in communion at all?
"Are you a magical creation?
"Have you nothing at all to give me, whether little or much?
If he says, "It should be given," one should say:
"Will you be able to grant the going forth? If he says no, one should not speak further; simply depart from there.
If he says, "I will be able," then it should be said:
"Did you go forth previously?
If he says, "I went forth," one should say:
"Have you fallen into any one of the four *pārājika* offenses?"
Or, if someone who has turned back from the training says to you, "I have fallen into an offense," you should say, "In that case, go. But if he says, "No," you should say,
"Is there anyone else who has gone forth at present?"
If he says, "I have gone forth," it should be asked:
"Has the holy life been lived correctly? "It has been lived.
"What is your name? "My name is so-and-so."
"What is the name of your preceptor? "I mention his name for a specific purpose;
my preceptor is named so-and-so."
Listen, venerable one: there indeed arise in men such bodily afflictions in the body as these,
namely, leprosy, boils, and so forth.
Scabies, leucoderma, and ringworm.
Eruptions on the ears and armpits, silver-colored [skin lesions], and scabies.
Hiccups, vomiting, and choleraic pain.
Lohaliṅgā, blood, and bile.
Abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano, and piles.
cough, dyspnea, and consumption.
epilepsy, aṭakkara, and jaundice;
breaking of a limb, breaking of a bone,
breaking of the ribs;
Obstruction of urine, diarrhea, elephantiasis, and discharge from the lungs.
continuous fever, quotidian fever, and tertian fever;
tertian fever, quartan fever, and fever arising from the combination of all three humors.
Continuous fever, intermittent fever, and the destruction of pride.
Such bodily ailments as these exist in the body,
or others of a similar kind;
that which was just now asked of me by you, they ask of you right here in the midst of the Saṅgha, [your] fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
In that regard, being confident, you must speak what is true as true and clarify what is untrue as untrue.
Stay; do not come while making improper sounds.
Thereafter, the monk acting as the private instructor, standing in the interior path, should say: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen!"
I, [name], shall train myself accordingly. [Name], with [name] as your preceptor—when someone is approaching, you should speak thus:
"If he is pure.
If it is so, then whoever seeks ordination should approach.
He should cause him to take up those practices that are not to be transgressed;
having taken them up, the three goings for refuge and the five precepts of the lay practitioner's restraint (upāsaka-saṃvara) should be conferred.
And furthermore, it should be given in this way:
"Pay attention, Venerable Sir! I, named so-and-so, go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of two-legged beings;
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the foremost of those free from passion."
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of assemblies.
May the Venerable One accept me as a lay follower for as long as life lasts.
This should be recited thus a second and a third time.
Pay attention, Preceptor!

Just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life—even so I, [name], having abandoned the taking of life for as long as life lasts, am abstaining from the taking of life. If they say this, it is well.
If they do not say this, they become guilty of an offense.

Thereafter, the monk who performs the ritual must have [the candidate] perform the proper salutation (sāmīcī), have him squat with his heels together in front [of the assembly], and have him raise his joined palms; then he must be made to request ordination.
And it should be requested in this manner:
Venerable sirs, may the Saṃgha listen. I, named so-and-so— I mention my name for a specific purpose— am desirous of full ordination with the preceptor named so-and-so.
I, [name], request full ordination from the Saṅgha. For the sake of clarity, I state my name:
may the venerable Saṅgha grant me full ordination with [name] as my preceptor.
May the venerable Saṅgha lift me up;
may the venerable Saṅgha favor me;
may the venerable Saṅgha have compassion for me.
Out of compassion, [the monk] should speak thus a second and a third time.
Thereafter, the monk acting as the ritual officiant (*karmakāraka*) must perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) by means of a vote (*muktikā*):
"Venerable sirs, may the Saṃgha listen."
This person, named so-and-so, seeking full ordination with the preceptor named so-and-so,
requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with such-and-such a preceptor.
If it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize the preceptor named so-and-so to question this person, named so-and-so, regarding the obstructing factors within the midst of the Saṅgha.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Thereafter, it should be said:
"Listen, venerable one! This is your time for truth; as before, up to: 'if others of this same kind exist.'"
Thereafter, having made the motion (jñapti), the formal act (karman) should be performed.
And it should be performed in this way:
"Listen, venerable Saṃghas!"
This person, named so-and-so, seeking full ordination with the preceptor named so-and-so,
is twenty years of age;
his three robes and alms bowl are complete.
He declares himself pure regarding the obstructing factors. This person, of such-and-such a name, with such-and-such a name as preceptor, requests full ordination from the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, [let it grant it].
The Saṃgha should grant permission: "Let the Saṃgha ordain the one named so-and-so with such-and-such a name as preceptor.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act (*karman*) should be performed in this manner.
Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This person, named so-and-so, seeking full ordination with the preceptor named so-and-so, is twenty years of age; his three robes and his alms-bowl are complete.
He declares himself to be pure regarding the obstructing factors.

This person, of such-and-such a name, with such-and-such a name as preceptor, requests full ordination from the Saṃgha; therefore, the Saṃgha grants full ordination to this person of such-and-such a name, with such-and-such a name as preceptor.
It is pleasing to those venerable ones.

"Let those who consent to ordaining the one named so-and-so with the preceptor named so-and-so remain silent; let those who do not consent speak. This is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*);
the second and third formal proclamations should be recited in the same manner."
The Saṃgha has conferred full ordination upon [so-and-so] with [so-and-so] as preceptor; it is approved and permitted by the Saṃgha, since there is silence. Thus do I understand this to be.
Thereafter, the shadow must be measured.
It was said by the Blessed One: "The shadow must be measured."
The monks measured [the distance] by steps, and it took too long.
The Blessed One said:
"It should not be measured by steps."
"It should be measured with a measuring-stake.
The monks measured it with one that was too long;
consequently, it took far too long.
The Blessed One said: "It should be measured with a peg four finger-breadths long.
As many pegs as there are, so many persons should be declared."
Thereafter, the time must be announced:
whether it is the forenoon, midday, or afternoon.
The first half-watch of the night is one watch; the middle half-watch is one watch;
the final half-watch is one watch.
The sun has not yet risen; the sun has risen;
the sun has not yet risen.
The sun has risen;
it has risen by one-eighth part from its initial position;
the sun has risen by one-fourth part.
The midday has not yet passed;
the midday has passed;
one quarter of the day remains; one eighth of the day remains.
The sun has not yet set;
the sun has set.
The stars have not yet risen; the stars have risen.
Thereafter, the *samaya* (seasonal period) should be announced.
There are five *samayas*: the winter (*haimantika*),...
the summer, the rainy season, and the post-rainy season;
The long rainy season consists of four months:
the winter months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Māgha, and Phālguna.
The summer season consists of four months:
Caitra, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, and Āṣāḍha.
The rainy season month is Śrāvaṇa.

The short rainy season (*mṛtavārṣika*) consists of one night and day, beginning on the first day of the month of Bhādrapada. The long rainy season (*dīrghavārṣika*) consists of three months minus one night.
[The months of] Bhādrapada, Āśvayuja, and Kārttika.
Thereafter, the four reliances (niśraya) should be announced:
"Listen, Venerable One! These four [reliances] were taught by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, who knows and sees."
Thus have the dependencies for a monk who has gone forth and received full ordination been declared—
those depending upon which there is the going forth, the full ordination, and the state of a monk within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya. What are the four?

Among robes, the rag-robe (*pāṃsukūla*) is both allowable and easily obtained; it is by depending upon this that a monk’s going-forth, full ordination, and status as a monk exist within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
Are you, [Name], able to subsist for as long as life lasts on a rag-robe as your clothing?
He should say: "I am able."

If an extra gain should arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual— whether it be a cloth-strip, a woven cloth, a fine cloth, a silk cloth, a *kauśeya* cloth, a *dukūla* cloth, a linen cloth, a *kauṭumbaka* cloth, a *sāloka* cloth, a cotton cloth, an *āmila* cloth, a *vāmila* cloth, a *sāmila* cloth, a *kṛmila* cloth,

a *kṛmivarṇa* cloth, a *samavarṇa* cloth, a golden-colored cloth, a dark-colored cloth, a fine *kāśika* cloth, a fine linen cloth, a fine *dukūla* cloth, a fine *kauṭumbaka* cloth, or whatever other suitable robe-material may arise— therein you must exercise moderation in acceptance.
"Will you attain such a state?
He should reply, "I will attain it.

"Listen: such-and-such a person, by means of alms-food—which is appropriate and easily obtained among foods—will undertake the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya."
"Are you able to subsist for as long as life lasts on alms-food alone?
He should reply, "I am able.

Extra gains—whether meals, or refreshments, or rice-gruel, or drinks, whether regular, or by invitation, or on the fifth day, or on the eighth day, or on the fourteenth day, or on the fifteenth day—[are permitted].

Whether it be an alms-offering that is accidental, or one that is a collection, or whatever other suitable alms-food may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual—in that case as well, you must exercise moderation in receiving it. [If asked:
"Will you be able to master such a state?
he should say: "I shall master it."

Listen: such is the name of the bedding and seating at the foot of trees, which is both suitable and easily obtained, depending upon which a monk’s going forth, full ordination, and status as a bhikṣu occur within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Are you, [Name], able to subsist throughout your life with bedding and seating at the foot of trees?
He should say: "I am able."

Extraneous acquisitions include: dwellings, or huts, or gabled houses, or small mansions, or upper chambers, or palaces, or attic rooms, or *āmalaka*-shaped structures, or earthen caves, or mountain caves, or cliff-side caves;
or shelters made of bamboo, or shelters made of leaves, or grass huts, or leaf huts; or prepared walkways, or unprepared walkways; or prepared overhangs, or unprepared overhangs.
Thus, whatever other suitable bedding or seating may arise from the Saṅgha or from an individual, you should exercise moderation in accepting it. If someone says, "Will you undertake such a position?
you should say, "I shall undertake it."
Listen, [Name]!

That which has been prescribed as medicine—suitable, appropriate, and easily obtained—relying upon which a monk’s going forth, full ordination, and status as a bhikṣu occurs within this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya:
are you, [Name], able to subsist for as long as life lasts on such prescribed medicine?
He should say: "I am able.
The extra acquisitions are: ghee, oil, honey, and molasses;
those to be used within a specific time—whether for a day, a watch of the night, a week, or as long as life lasts.

Root medicine, stem medicine, leaf medicine, flower medicine, fruit medicine, or whatever other suitable medicine there may be—whether it arises from the Saṅgha or from an individual—in that case as well, you must exercise moderation in accepting it. If you should perceive such a situation, you should say: "I shall accept it."
[The Four Defeats: Thereafter, the four dharmas involving defeat (patanīya-dharma) must be announced.
Furthermore, they should be announced in this manner:

"Listen, you named so-and-so! These four dharmas involving defeat have been declared by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—who knows and sees—concerning a monk who has thus gone forth and received full ordination."
The dharmas have been declared.
Should a monk fall into any one of these states, by that very falling he ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, ceases to be a son of the Śākyas.
He is destroyed from his state of monkhood; his status as a hearer is slain, ruined, shattered, fallen, and defeated; his life as a śramaṇa becomes irrecoverable.
Which four?
In many ways, venerable sir, the Blessed One has censured sensual pleasures;
he has praised the abandoning of sensual pleasures and the lack of attachment to sensual pleasures.
It is relinquishment, it is vomiting out;
it is destruction, dispassion, cessation, subsiding; it is easy to practice, praised, lauded, extolled, and commended.
From this day forward, O Venerable One, you must not look upon a woman with a lustful mind, nor gaze at her with a mind bound by desire.
How much more so, then, to engage in unchaste sexual intercourse through the union of two by two?
And this has been said, O Venerable One, by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksambuddha, who knows and sees:

"If a monk, having entered into the training and proper conduct together with other monks, should engage in unchaste sexual intercourse without having renounced the training and without having disclosed his weakness in the training..."

Even for one who has gone to the animal realm, if a monk, having committed such an act as "together with her," commits it along with her, he ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, ceases to be a son of the Śākyas;
he falls from the state of a monk.
His śramaṇahood is destroyed; his śramaṇahood is ruined, crushed, fallen, defeated, and cannot be recovered.

Just as a palmyra tree whose head has been cut off is incapable of becoming green again, incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion, even so, a monk who has committed such an offense, having committed it, finds that his state of being a recluse must be relinquished.

Therefore, from this day forward, while you are practicing meditation through the conduct of presence, you must apply yourself even more intensely to the restraint of improper conduct during meditation. You must apply yourself to mindfulness and vigilance,
lest you should fall into such a state.
He should say: "I shall not commit [this offense].
Listen, venerable one, in many ways the Blessed One has censured the taking of what is not given;
the abstention from taking what is not given has been praised, extolled, lauded, and commended."
"From this day forward, venerable one, you must not, with a mind of theft, take even a sesame husk belonging to another that has not been given; how much less so five māṣas or more than five māṣas?
And this was said, venerable one, by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha—who knows and sees:
'Whatever monk should, whether in a village or in the wilderness, take what belongs to others and has not been given, in such a way as to constitute theft.'"
If a monk, having committed an act of taking what is not given such that the king or the king’s minister, upon seizing him, would execute him, imprison him, or banish him, and would say of him:
"O man, you are a thief! You are a fool! You are a deluded one! You are a robber!"—by committing such an offense, and by having committed it, he ceases to be a monk, he ceases to be a śramaṇa.
Just as a palm tree whose crown is severed cannot recover, so too [he cannot recover] until he has confessed it.
Listen, Venerable One! In many ways the Blessed One has censured the taking of life;

he has praised, extolled, lauded, and commended the abstention from taking life. From this day forward, Venerable One, you must not intentionally deprive any living being of life, even one as small as an ant, let alone a human being or one in human form. And it was said by the Venerable One:

By the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha—it was declared: "If a monk, with his own hand, intentionally deprives a human being or one in human form of life; or if he provides him with a weapon, or seeks for him one who provides a weapon;
or if he incites him toward death..."
Or he would describe the praises of death to him,
and speak to him thus: "O man, what is the use of this evil, impure, and wretched life?"
"O man, it is better for you to be dead than to live. Thus,
with thoughts approved by his own mind and mental intentions, he might incite him to death in various ways, or describe the praises of death to him, and he might die because of that.
Having fallen into such a state, a monk, by that very fall, ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, and ceases to be a son of the Śākyas.
[As stated] previously, up to: "I shall not fall into it.
Listen, venerable one: in many ways the Blessed One has censured false speech.
Abstaining from false speech has been praised, extolled, described, and lauded.
From this day forward, O Venerable One, even for the sake of a joke, you must not speak a falsehood while being fully aware of it;
how much less so should you practice claiming a superior human state that is actually non-existent?
"Indeed, O Venerable One, this was said by that Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha—who knows and sees:
'If a monk, being without it and not possessing it, should claim a superior human state, a distinction of the noble ones, an attainment, knowledge, vision, or a state of dwelling in comfort, saying:
"I know this; I see this," [he commits an offense]. "
What do I know? I know suffering; I know its origin, its cessation, and the path.
What do I see?
I see the gods;
I see the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas.
The gods also see me.
Nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, pretas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even kaṭapūtanas see me.
I hear the voices of the gods;
I hear the voices of the nāgas, yakṣas, and kaṭapūtanas.
Even the gods hear my voice;
the nāgas, yakṣas, and kaṭapūtanas also hear my voice.
I approach in order to see the gods.
I approach for the sake of seeing the nāgas, yakṣas, and kaṭapūtanas;
even the gods approach me for the sake of seeing me.
I converse with the gods, chat with them, exchange greetings with them, and even enter into continuous discourse with them.

I converse with and exchange greetings with the nāgas and yakṣas, even engaging in constant discourse with them. The gods also converse with me, speak with me, exchange greetings, and even engage in constant discourse with me.
The nāgas, yakṣas, and kaṭapūtanas also converse with me, exchange greetings, and even engage in constant discourse with me.
He claims of himself, "I am one who has attained the perception of impermanence," though he has not yet attained it;
likewise regarding the perception of suffering in the impermanent,
the perception of non-self in what is suffering, and the perception of repulsiveness in food.

He claims of himself: "I am one who has attained the perception of non-delight in all the world, the perception of disadvantage, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, and the perception of the foul regarding what was previously unattained. He claims of himself: "I am one who has attained the perception of the livid corpse, the perception of the festering corpse, the perception of the worm-infested corpse, the perception of the skeletal corpse, and the perception of the contemplation of emptiness."
Not attaining mastery over the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyāna;
over loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*);

over the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); nor over the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).

If a monk, apart from mere overestimation, claims for himself that he possesses the range of supernormal powers, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, recollection of past lives, knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and the destruction of the outflows— claiming to be one who dwells in the eight liberations through meditation, though he is neither a non-arahant nor an arahant and has not performed the necessary actions— then by falling into such a state and persisting in it, he ceases to be a monk, ceases to be a śramaṇa, ceases to be a son of the Śākyas; he is fallen from the state of a monk, and his status as a śramaṇa is destroyed.
His ascetic life (*śrāmaṇya*) becomes destroyed, crushed, fallen, defeated, and irrecoverable.
Just as a palm tree whose crown is severed is incapable of becoming green again, and incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion,
even so a monk who has committed such an offense, having committed it, finds his ascetic life to be irrecoverable.

Therefore, in this regard, while reflecting with a forward-directed mind upon the non-transgression of conduct and the abstention from transgressions of conduct, one must apply oneself even more intensely to mindfulness and vigilance.
One should think: "I shall not fall into such a state," and thus declare: "I shall not fall into it."
[The four qualities that make one a recluse: Thereafter, the four qualities that make one a recluse (*śramaṇakāraka-dharma*) should be announced.
Furthermore, they should be announced in this way:
"Listen, venerable one! These four qualities that make one a recluse have been proclaimed by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who knows and sees."
Which four?
From this day forward, venerable one, you must not revile one who reviles you;
you must not strike back at one who strikes you.
When one has been reviled, one should not revile in return; when one has been angered, one should not anger in return. "Will you commit such an act?"—to this he should say, "I will not commit it.
"Listen, venerable sir! Long ago there was a certain horse-trainer..."
"May I obtain the going forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
You have now gone forth and received full ordination with a suitable preceptor.
By two suitable preceptors,
by a complete Saṃgha,
through a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth proclamation.
[This applies] to one who is unshakable and not subject to formal re-establishment.
In that which must be trained in by a monk ordained for a hundred years, there [must be training] by one ordained on that very day.
Regarding "by one ordained for a hundred years," this refers to the equality of conduct, the equality of training, and the equality of the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
From this day forward, you must neither please him nor displease him.
From this day forward, you should maintain the perception of your preceptor as a father, and your preceptor should likewise maintain the perception of you as a son.
From this day forward, you must attend upon your preceptor for as long as life lasts.
Your preceptor, in turn, must attend upon you when you are ill, until either death occurs or recovery is achieved.

From this day forward, you must dwell with reverence toward your fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether they be seniors, those of middle standing, or juniors—and remain under their guidance with respect, deference, and a sense of awe.
From this day forward, you must teach it, recite it, and study it.
Skillfulness regarding the aggregates should be cultivated;
skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding the sense bases,
and skillfulness regarding dependent origination.
Skill in what is possible and what is impossible;
furthermore, he should train in this for the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained.
For the attainment of what has not been attained; for the realization of what has not been realized. And these gross rules of training have been declared to you by me.
Furthermore, we shall hear other matters when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is recited every half-month;

and other teachers, preceptors, co-residents with the same preceptor, those with the same teacher, close associates, intimate friends, and those who are affectionate toward one another will cause you to grasp them as well.
Thus have you been ordained in the teaching of the One of Excellent Wisdom;
do not let this rare endowment of the opportune moment go to waste.
"For one who is pleasing, the going forth and the pure full ordination have been proclaimed by the Truly Named One, the Fully Awakened One, who possesses true knowledge."
Venerable one, you who have received the full ordination through this Dharma, accomplish it with diligence.
The formal motion for full ordination is concluded.
